questions.question: Two rules target the same element with the same specificity, setting the same property differently. Which wins?
options: The one written earlier in the stylesheet
The one written later in source order
The one containing more declarations
The browser picks one at random
questions.rationale: When origin and specificity tie, the cascade falls through to source order: the last matching declaration wins.

questions.question: Which selector wins: #signup or .card p?
options: #signup, because an id (1-0-0) outweighs any number of classes and elements
.card p, because it is more specific about structure
They tie and source order decides
It depends on which element is being styled
questions.rationale: Specificity compares ids first, then classes, then elements: 1-0-0 beats 0-1-1 regardless of source order.

questions.question: With box-sizing: border-box, what does a declared width include?
options: The content only
The content plus the margin
The content plus padding plus border
Everything including the margin
questions.rationale: border-box makes the declared width the outer edge of the border, carving padding and border out of it; margin always stays outside the box.

questions.question: A paragraph with margin-bottom: 20px sits above one with margin-top: 30px. How much vertical space separates them?
options: 50px, the margins add up
20px, the smaller margin wins
10px, the margins cancel
30px — adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger of the two
questions.rationale: Adjacent block margins collapse: the gap is the maximum of the two, which is why styling one margin direction avoids surprises.

questions.question: In a flex container, which axis does justify-content control?
options: The cross axis
The main axis
Both axes at once
Neither — it controls z-order
questions.rationale: justify-content distributes items along the main axis (horizontal by default), while align-items handles the perpendicular cross axis.

questions.question: In CSS grid, what does the fr unit mean?
options: A fixed rem-based measurement
Frames per second of the layout animation
A fraction of the leftover free space
A font-relative ratio
questions.rationale: fr distributes free space proportionally, so 1fr 2fr gives the second track twice the leftover width after fixed tracks are laid out.

questions.question: What does writing CSS mobile-first mean in practice?
options: Base styles for small screens, then add min-width media queries as space allows
Design for desktop first, then patch with max-width queries
Build a separate website for each device class
Use only pixel units so phones scale automatically
questions.rationale: Mobile-first starts from the narrow layout and layers on enhancements with min-width queries, which keeps the base CSS simple and respects the viewport meta.

questions.question: What is the essential difference between flexbox and grid?
options: Flexbox is two-dimensional while grid is one-dimensional
Grid is one-dimensional while flexbox is two-dimensional
They cannot be combined on the same page
Flexbox lays out one axis at a time, while grid arranges rows and columns together
questions.rationale: Flexbox is a one-dimensional tool (a row or a column, content-driven), grid is two-dimensional (tracks defined up front), and the two are typically combined.

questions.question: What does the fallback value in var(--brand, #333) do?
options: Uses #333 when --brand is not defined in scope
Always overrides --brand with #333
Raises an error because two values are present
Defines --brand permanently as #333
questions.rationale: The second argument of var is used only when the custom property is missing, which makes components robust to partial theming.

questions.question: How does position: sticky behave?
options: Always pinned to the viewport, ignoring the flow
Removed from the flow like absolute
It scrolls with the flow until a threshold is crossed, then behaves like fixed
It is identical to position: relative
questions.rationale: Sticky stays in normal flow until the scroll position passes the set offset, then sticks — the classic table header or section title behavior.
